new_statements.quote: Cabe resaltar que los promedios de la Tabla 9 no discriminan si una vocal es acentuada o no o si esta aparece en sílaba inicial o final de palabra puesto que el acento tiende a ubicarse en la última sílaba. (p. 107) ... En conclusión, las vocales acentuadas en arabela son un poco más extremas que las vocales inacentuadas y estas a su vez tienden a centralizarse (p. 113) ... En términos generales, las vocales acentuadas poseen mayor duración que las vocales inacentuadas en ambos sexos. (p. 119)
new_statements.translation: It should be noted that the averages in Table 9 do not distinguish whether a vowel is stressed or not, or whether it occurs in word-initial or word-final syllable, since the stress tends to be located on the last syllable. (p. 107) ... In conclusion, stressed vowels in Arabela are somewhat more peripheral than unstressed vowels, and the latter in turn tend to centralize (p. 113) ... In general terms, stressed vowels are longer than unstressed vowels in both sexes. (p. 119)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records fixed initial stress; Jiménez says stress tends to be final. This is an aside in a segmental thesis, not a demonstrated analysis, but it is the only explicit placement statement found for this language in the opened sources.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress 'tends to' fall on the last syllable of the word; stated in passing while explaining why vowel-formant averages were not split by stress or position. Stressed vowels are longer (by roughly 0.010-0.040 s) and more peripheral. The thesis is a segmental phonology and has no stress or prosody section; it does not say how stressed syllables were identified.
new_statements.exceptions: 'tiende a' (tends to) only; no exceptions listed. Elsewhere the author suggests /k/ lenition and [ɾ]~[r] variation may be prosodically conditioned (pp. 204, 243) and cites Rich (1999:14) on unstressed vowels being lost between homorganic consonants (p. 226).
new_statements.identity_note: Jiménez 2018 describes the Arabela of the río Arabela (Buena Vista community), Napo district, Maynas, Loreto, based on instrumental recordings of several men and women. Wauters' materials were recorded May-July 2012 in Buena Vista and Santa Clotilde (Napo, Maynas, Loreto) with Edgar Pastor Rosero, Nelly Pastor Rosero and other Rosero-family consultants; same variety, same community. Rich 1975 (SIL) is on the same language but was not opened.

readall_conflicts: The catalog records fixed initial stress (source StressTyp2). The one explicit placement statement opened, Jiménez 2018 p. 107, says stress 'tends to be located on the last syllable' (final), the opposite edge. Wauters' 2012 field transcriptions (CLA 2016-08, FLEx export) mark stress initially in most 2-3-syllable forms, which supports the catalog against Jiménez for short words, but in 4-5-syllable forms she marks primary stress on the third syllable with a secondary mark on the first, and long-vowel syllables attract the primary mark; her notes say 'stress moves' and 'tone and accent are somewhat variable'. Rich 1975 could not be opened (SIL an automated-access block block), so it neither confirms nor refutes any of these.
